lesson.title: When Code Breaks: A Field Guide to the Three Kinds of Errors
lesson.summary: Every broken program falls into one of three very different categories, caught before it runs, caught while it runs, or not caught at all, and telling them apart is the first real debugging skill.
lesson.body:
Every programmer, no matter how experienced, writes code that breaks. What separates a beginner from an experienced programmer is not that experienced programmers avoid mistakes, it is that they recognize quickly which of three very different kinds of "broken" they are looking at, because each kind is diagnosed and fixed in a completely different way. This chapter is a map of that territory. Each of the three categories gets its own dedicated chapter right after this one, so think of this as the overview that tells you why the distinction matters before you dig into the details of each.

The first category is a syntax error. Before Python runs any of your code, it first reads through the whole file and checks that it follows Python's grammar rules, things like every function definition ending its header line with a colon, every open parenthesis eventually being closed, and so on. If your code breaks one of these rules, Python refuses to run any of it at all, not even the lines before the mistake, and it reports a SyntaxError instead. This is the category caught earliest: before the program ever starts.

The second category is a runtime error, more commonly called an exception. Here the code is completely valid Python grammar, so the program does start running, but partway through, some line tries to do something that turns out to be impossible given the actual data at that moment, dividing a number by zero, for instance. When that happens, Python stops the program right at that line and prints a traceback, a report showing exactly where things went wrong. This category is caught while the program is running, and it always comes with a visible error message.

```python
def average(numbers):
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)

print(average([]))
```

Running this prints a traceback whose final line is:

```
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
```

The syntax here is perfectly valid, Python has no complaint about how the code is written, so it starts running normally. It is only when this particular call passes an empty list, making len(numbers) equal to 0, that dividing by that length becomes impossible, and Python raises the exception at that exact line. Call average([10, 20, 30]) instead and this same code runs without any error at all, which is the signature trait of a runtime error: whether it happens depends on the data flowing through the code at the moment it runs, not on how the code itself is written.

The third category is the sneakiest: a logic error. Here the code has valid syntax and runs from start to finish with no crash and no traceback at all, it produces an answer and looks completely successful. The only problem is that the answer is wrong, because the code does not actually do what the programmer intended, even though it does exactly what the programmer wrote. Python has no way to flag this, because Python has no idea what result you meant to get, it only executes the instructions you gave it. This is why logic errors are, in a real sense, the hardest of the three to catch: there is no error message to point you at the problem, so you have to notice on your own that an answer is wrong.

Later in this course you will also learn how to use a try/except block to catch a runtime error yourself and keep your program running instead of letting it crash, and you will learn that every exception is actually an object with a specific type name attached to it. For now, the goal is simpler: whenever something goes wrong, the first question to ask is which of these three categories you are looking at, because that decides where to even start looking for the bug.
